title: Can the `main()` method be overloaded, and which signature does the JVM actually use as the entry point?
shortTitle: Can the main method be overloaded?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, the main method can be overloaded like any other method, meaning a class may declare several methods named main with different parameter lists, and they all compile legally. However, the Java Virtual Machine launcher uses one and only one of them as the application entry point: the method whose signature is exactly public static void main of a single String array. The other overloads are ordinary methods that the JVM ignores at startup; they only run if some code explicitly calls them. So overloading main is permitted and sometimes useful as helper methods, but it never changes which signature starts the program.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine the branch has several doors all labelled main, but only one of them, the one of a very specific standard shape, is the official opening-time entrance that head office uses. The bank can build as many other doors labelled main as it likes, of different shapes, and staff may use them during the day for internal purposes, but head office, meaning the JVM, will only ever open the branch through the one door with the exact standard shape, public static void main taking a String array. The extra doors exist and work, but they never serve as the morning entrance unless someone inside the branch deliberately walks through them.
s1_definition.oneliner: You can overload main freely, but the JVM only ever uses public static void main of a String array as the entry point, and all other overloads are ignored at startup unless your code explicitly calls them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, the main method can be overloaded like any other method, meaning a class may declare several methods named main with different parameter lists, and they all compile legally. However, the Java Virtual Machine launcher uses one and only one of them as the application entry point: the method whose signature is exactly public static void main of a single String array. The other overloads are ordinary methods that the JVM ignores at startup; they only run if some code explicitly calls them. So overloading main is permitted and sometimes useful as helper methods, but it never changes which signature starts the program.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine the branch has several doors all labelled main, but only one of them, the one of a very specific standard shape, is the official opening-time entrance that head office uses. The bank can build as many other doors labelled main as it likes, of different shapes, and staff may use them during the day for internal purposes, but head office, meaning the JVM, will only ever open the branch through the one door with the exact standard shape, public static void main taking a String array. The extra doors exist and work, but they never serve as the morning entrance unless someone inside the branch deliberately walks through them.

**One line to remember:** You can overload main freely, but the JVM only ever uses public static void main of a String array as the entry point, and all other overloads are ignored at startup unless your code explicitly calls them.

sections.s2_technical:
Overloading means declaring multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, and main is not special in this respect. So a class can legally contain public static void main of a String array, plus public static void main of an int, plus public static void main with no parameters, plus public static void main of two strings. All of these compile because they differ in parameters, which is exactly what overloading allows.

The JVM launcher, however, resolves the entry point by an exact signature match, not by name alone. It requires public access, the static modifier, a void return type, the method name main, and exactly one parameter of type String array. When you run the class, the launcher invokes precisely that method. If the class does not contain that exact signature, the JVM reports that it cannot find or load a main method, even if other methods named main are present.

The other overloads behave like normal methods. They never run automatically at startup. They run only if something calls them, and a very common and tidy pattern is for the real entry point to delegate to an overload. For example the entry point might parse the String array arguments and then call an overloaded main of parsed, typed parameters, keeping the argument-handling separate from the business logic. That overload is just a regular method that happens to share the name.

Several senior points matter. First, the return type and access do not participate in overload resolution within Java, but they do matter to the JVM's entry-point rule, so a method named main that is public static but returns int rather than void is a legal overload yet is not a valid entry point. Second, because varargs String compiles to a String array, a main declared with varargs is accepted by the JVM as the entry point, and you cannot have both public static void main of a String array and public static void main of varargs String in the same class, because they have the same erased signature and would clash. Third, overloading is resolved at compile time based on the static types of the arguments, so when the entry point calls an overloaded main, the compiler picks the version matching the argument types you pass. In banking batch tools this is a clean way to structure a launcher: the JVM-facing main unpacks command-line arguments, and an overloaded main of strongly typed parameters does the actual settlement, which is easier to unit test because tests call the typed overload directly without constructing a raw argument array.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank's settlement launcher must be startable by the JVM, so it needs the one exact entry-point signature, but the team also wants a cleaner, strongly typed method for the real logic. This is exactly where overloading main helps: one overload is the JVM entry point and another is the typed worker.

Problem 2 — The test team wants to run the settlement logic directly without building a raw string array of fake command-line arguments. This is exactly why the typed overloaded main is useful and testable.

Problem 3 — A developer wondered whether adding a second main of different parameters would confuse the JVM at startup, and the answer is no, because the JVM only matches the exact String array signature. This is exactly the entry-point resolution rule.

The code is an `OverloadedMainDemo` class with the real JVM entry point main of a String array, an overloaded main of typed parameters that it delegates to, and another harmless overloaded main, all demonstrating that only the String array version starts the program.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
overloaded-main-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/batch/
│       └── OverloadedMainDemo.java   (JVM entry main + overloaded mains)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/batch/OverloadedMainDemo.java

# Run — the JVM invokes ONLY main(String[]); overloads run only via explicit calls
java -cp out com.bank.batch.OverloadedMainDemo CUR3001 75000.00
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: command-line arguments CUR3001 and 75000.00 supplied after the class name.

Step 1 — The JVM loads the class and looks for the exact entry-point signature. Although the class contains four methods named main, the launcher selects only public static void main of a String array, ignoring the others at startup.

Step 2 — The entry-point main receives the arguments in the String array, reads the account id from index zero as CUR3001, and parses the amount from index one as seventy five thousand, applying defaults if they were absent.

Step 3 — The entry-point main then explicitly calls the overloaded main that takes a String and a BigDecimal. This is ordinary overload resolution happening at compile time based on the argument types, and it has nothing to do with the JVM entry-point rule; it is simply a method call.

Step 4 — The typed overload logs the settlement of seventy five thousand for CUR3001 and would run the real business logic. Because it takes typed parameters, a unit test could call it directly without building a fake argument array.

Step 5 — The other two overloads, one taking an int and one taking a boolean and returning int, are never invoked by the JVM and would only run if some code called them. The int-returning one is a reminder that a method named main that does not return void is a valid overload but not a valid entry point.

Step 6 — The output shows the entry point firing first, then the typed overload performing the settlement, proving that overloading is allowed while the JVM still uses only the String array signature to start.

```
Oct 30, 2026 5:00:41 PM com.bank.batch.OverloadedMainDemo main
INFO: JVM entry point: public static void main(String[]) invoked by the launcher.
Oct 30, 2026 5:00:41 PM com.bank.batch.OverloadedMainDemo main
INFO: Overload main(String, BigDecimal): settling Rs.75000.00 for CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  $ java OverloadedMainDemo CUR3001 75000.00

    ▼
  JVM launcher: scan class for entry point
    ├─ main(String[])          ← EXACT match → CHOSEN

    └─ main(boolean):int       ← ignored (not void anyway)

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, the main method can be overloaded, because overloading simply means having several methods with the same name but different parameter lists, and main is not special in that regard. A class can legally declare public static void main of a String array alongside a main that takes an int, a main that takes two strings, or a main with any other parameters, and they all compile fine. What overloading never changes is which method starts the program.

The Java Virtual Machine launcher resolves the entry point by an exact signature, not by the name alone. It requires public access, the static modifier, a void return type, the name main, and exactly one parameter of type String array. That precise signature is the one and only method the JVM invokes at startup. If the class does not contain it, the JVM reports that it cannot find a main method, regardless of how many other methods named main exist. All the other overloads are ordinary methods that run only if some code explicitly calls them.

I actually use this deliberately in banking batch tools. The JVM-facing main of a String array does nothing but unpack the command-line arguments, choosing the account id and amount, and then it delegates by calling an overloaded main that takes strongly typed parameters such as a String account id and a BigDecimal amount. That typed overload holds the real settlement logic. The big practical benefit is testability: a unit test can call the typed overload directly with real objects instead of constructing a fake array of string arguments, which makes the tests cleaner and more focused.

The senior nuances I add are that overload resolution happens at compile time based on the static types of the arguments, so when the entry point calls the typed main, the compiler picks the matching overload. Also, because a varargs String parameter compiles to the same String array type, a main declared with varargs is accepted by the JVM as the entry point, and for that same reason you cannot declare both a String array main and a varargs String main in one class, since their erased signatures clash. And a method named main that returns int rather than void is a perfectly legal overload but is not a valid entry point, so the JVM would still look for the void String array version. Understanding that overloading is free but the entry-point signature is fixed is what lets me structure launchers that are both JVM-startable and easy to test.

---

keyPoints: Yes — you can have main(int x), main(String s), etc.
JVM only calls main(String[] args) as the entry point
Other main overloads are just regular methods, called manually
Overloading main is valid Java but confusing in practice
